warmup.q: The reflective container wires a 14-component box office with one JDK proxy and one Byte Buddy subclass. Roughly how many classes does that JVM load before the first ticket is sold?
options: About 30: the 14 components and a few container classes
About 1,000, the same as any small Java program
warmup.why: On JDK 21 the reflective start loaded 2,207 classes: 814 of them from the Byte Buddy JAR, 30 JDK proxy classes, 3 classes Byte Buddy wrote, and over a hundred hidden classes for lambdas and method handles. The same app wired by generated code loaded 991, which is the second option's number. Most of a container's start-up cost is the machinery, not your components.

opening:
Picture the box office computer restarting ten minutes before the doors open, with the queue already out on the street. The program has to be back before the first customer reaches the counter, and every start repeats the whole of lessons 1 and 2. It scans the classes, reads every annotation, checks the graph, and has Byte Buddy sew its costume copy.

Two numbers wait for us, and they point in opposite directions. A call through a stand-in costs a few hundred nanoseconds at most. A start with all that machinery loads more than twice as many classes as the same wiring written out as plain code. The easy trap is to measure only the first number, find it tiny, and call the proxies free.

The last lesson gave the container its stand-ins. In this one, we'll measure them per call and at start-up, and look inside the running container. Then we'll move the wiring to the build, and archive what's left. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with the box office computer restarting ten minutes before the doors open. A stand-in cost a few hundred bytes a call, the machinery behind it more than a thousand classes a start, and writing the wiring out at build time took most of that away.

Now run a program of your own with -Xlog:class+load, and count the classes it loads before its first request.

That ends Part 4. Part 1 kept a bank correct under many threads, Part 2 kept a post office counter answering while it waited, Part 3 gave a courier's events types the compiler checks, and Part 4 went backstage at the theatre, the warehouse and the kitchen.

Next, Part 5 takes today's last step all the way. Our registry was written by a small generator we ran by hand. What if the build itself read the annotations in your code and wrote such files every time, so they could never fall out of step?

sections.h: One call through a stand-in: nanoseconds and a couple of hundred bytes
sections.html:
Start with the cost of one call. Measuring a single call needs care. From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 pictured the JVM as a new cook. A fresh JVM reads every method from its recipe card, line by line, and cooks the busy ones from memory only later, with shortcuts. Time the first calls, and you've measured the cook's first day. So ProxyCallBench uses JMH, the OpenJDK project's benchmark harness. JMH runs a small piece of code in a fresh JVM and measures it only after the JIT compiler has done its work. (The JIT compiler is the part of the JVM that turns busy methods into machine code.) Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from called it the fair taste test: a warmed-up kitchen, a fresh JVM for each round, ingredients the cook can't predict, and a judge who eats every result. Here we return each result and read the input from a non-final field, so the JIT can neither throw the work away nor fold it into a constant. JMH's -prof gc option adds a second number: the bytes each call allocates, B/op.

The benchmark makes one booking-fee calculation four ways. Each chain holds a single interceptor that only calls proceed(), so the numbers are the stand-ins' own cost, and the direct call is the baseline. One run on this course's 4-core machine, which was busy with other builds at the time:

Call ns/op B/op
direct 1.4 0
generated forwarding class (this lesson) 2.3 0
Byte Buddy subclass (lesson 2) 69 160
JDK proxy (lesson 2) 239 208

Every error bar was larger than its score, so read the time column for its order only. The bytes held up better. Over four runs, the direct and generated rows stayed at 0, and the JDK proxy at 208 to 213 B/op, while its time went from about 110 ns to over 3,000. Byte Buddy's row moved between 64 and 160 B/op: these runs are short, and the JIT didn't remove the same objects on that path every time.

Where do 208 bytes come from? The JDK proxy's generated method boxes the long argument, wrapping it in a Long object, and puts it in an Object[]. The handler builds an Invocation for each step of the chain and a lambda for the target call, and Method.invoke boxes the result. The generated forwarding class does the same things in its source: new Object[] {p0}, new Invocation(...), a lambda. But its whole call is plain code that C2, the JIT's optimizing compiler, can inline: it copies each method the call reaches into the caller. Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics pictured that as the cook who copies the sauce from page 12 into the main recipe. Once inlined, none of those objects leaves the compiled method, and escape analysis, C2's check for objects that never leave the code it compiled, removes them all. Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis put it in the warehouse's words: a box that never leaves the desk is never made. On the two reflective paths, C2 couldn't see the whole call, so the objects stay.

Don't build on that zero. As the Try it shows, one more interceptor is enough to lose it. The Kotlin twin counts the same calls in a plain loop and gets 0, 208, 192 and 48 bytes: the same order, with less of the generated class's allocation removed.

Does any of it matter? At 2,000 booking calls a second, 208 bytes each is 400 KB of short-lived garbage a second, next to a network call that takes milliseconds: nothing. In a loop that prices 10,000 seats through a proxied PriceList, it's 2 MB for every pass. Put the stand-in in front of the booking service, not in front of the arithmetic. Per call, then, the stand-ins are cheap. The start is another matter.

code.title: ProxyCallBench.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l03.demo; import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.MethodDelegation; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.profile.GCProfiler; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import workbench.container.l03.InterceptingHandler; import workbench.container.l03.Interceptor; import workbench.container.l03.Invocation; import workbench.container.l03.SubclassBridge; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** * One booking-fee calculation, called directly and through the container's three kinds of interception. * Every chain holds one interceptor that only calls proceed(), so the numbers are the proxies' own cost, * and direct() is the baseline to compare against. * Short runs on a shared machine: read the order and the bytes, not the decimals. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 150, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 150, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class ProxyCallBench { public interface Prices { long feeCents(long priceCents); } public static class PlainPrices implements Prices { @Override public long feeCents(long priceCents) { return (priceCents * 29 + 500) / 1000; } } static final Interceptor PASS = Invocation::proceed; // does nothing but carry on static final List<Interceptor> CHAIN = List.of(PASS); /** A copy of the forwarding class RegistryGenerator writes for an intercepted interface. */ static final class Prices_Proxy implements Prices { private final Prices target; Prices_Proxy(Prices target) { this.target = target; } @Override public long feeCents(long p0) { return (Long) new Invocation("Prices.feeCents", new Object[] {p0}, CHAIN, () -> target.feeCents(p0)).proceed(); } } long price = 12_000; // non-final: the JIT can't fold it Prices direct, jdkProxy, byteBuddy, generated; @Setup public void setup() throws Exception { direct = new PlainPrices(); Method fee = Prices.class.getMethod("feeCents", long.class); jdkProxy = (Prices) Proxy.newProxyInstance(Prices.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {Prices.class}, new InterceptingHandler(new PlainPrices(), Map.of(fee, CHAIN))); byteBuddy = new ByteBuddy().subclass(PlainPrices.class) .method(named("feeCents")) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration().filter(named("intercept")) .to(new SubclassBridge(Map.of(PlainPrices.class.getMethod("feeCents", long.class), CHAIN)))) .make().load(PlainPrices.class.getClassLoader()).getLoaded() .getConstructor().newInstance(); generated = new Prices_Proxy(new PlainPrices()); } @Benchmark public long direct() { return direct.feeCents(price); } @Benchmark public long jdkProxy() { return jdkProxy.feeCents(price); } @Benchmark public long byteBuddy() { return byteBuddy.feeCents(price); } @Benchmark public long generated() { return generated.feeCents(price); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(ProxyCallBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) // the same as -prof gc .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-10s %9s %9s %9s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-10s %9.2f %9.2f %9.1f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore()); } } }

alt.html: package workbench.container.l03.demo // ProxyCallBench.java times these calls with JMH, which needs Java classes in this lab. This twin // makes the same four calls from Kotlin and counts the bytes each one allocates with the JVM's // per-thread allocation counter, after a warm-up so the JIT has compiled them. import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy import net.bytebuddy.implementation.MethodDelegation import net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named import workbench.container.l03.InterceptingHandler import workbench.container.l03.Interceptor import workbench.container.l03.Invocation import workbench.container.l03.SubclassBridge import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.lang.reflect.Proxy interface KPrices { fun feeCents(priceCents: Long): Long } open class KPlainPrices : KPrices { override fun feeCents(priceCents: Long) = (priceCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 } private val chain = listOf(Interceptor { it.proceed() }) // does nothing but carry on /** The shape RegistryGenerator writes for an intercepted interface. */ class KPricesProxy(private val target: KPrices) : KPrices { override fun feeCents(priceCents: Long): Long = Invocation("KPrices.feeCents", arrayOf(priceCents), chain) { target.feeCents(priceCents) }.proceed() as Long } private val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean private var sink = 0L // results go somewhere the JIT can't ignore // inline: every use gets its own call site, which sees one class, as each JMH benchmark does private inline fun bytesPerCall(call: (Long) -> Long): Double { repeat(200_000) { sink += call(12_000L + it % 3) } // warm up: let C2 compile the path val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(100_000) { sink += call(12_000L + it % 3) } return (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before).toDouble() / 100_000 } fun main() { val fee = KPrices::class.java.getMethod("feeCents", Long::class.java) val jdkProxy = Proxy.newProxyInstance(KPrices::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(KPrices::class.java), InterceptingHandler(KPlainPrices(), mapOf(fee to chain))) as KPrices val byteBuddy = ByteBuddy().subclass(KPlainPrices::class.java) .method(named("feeCents")) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration().filter(named("intercept")) .to(SubclassBridge(mapOf(KPlainPrices::class.java.getMethod("feeCents", Long::class.java) to chain)))) .make().load(KPlainPrices::class.java.classLoader).loaded .getConstructor().newInstance() val direct = KPlainPrices() val generated = KPricesProxy(KPlainPrices()) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("direct", bytesPerCall { direct.feeCents(it) })) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("jdkProxy", bytesPerCall { jdkProxy.feeCents(it) })) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("byteBuddy", bytesPerCall { byteBuddy.feeCents(it) })) println("%-10s %8.1f B/call".format("generated", bytesPerCall { generated.feeCents(it) })) println("(checksum $sink)") }

try.expect: direct and generated show 0.0 B/op and jdkProxy about 208. byteBuddy shows 160 in most runs, and less in some on a busy machine. Times jump around, with errors larger than the scores, but direct and generated stay within a few nanoseconds and the two reflective paths are far slower. With two interceptors, every row but direct allocates more. In one run the reflective rows grew by 32 bytes each (one more Invocation, to 192 and 240), and generated jumped from 0 to 128 B/op: with the longer chain, escape analysis no longer removed its objects. That's why Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis said to show escape analysis in demos and never assert it in tests. The Kotlin twin prints 0, 208, 192 and 48 bytes per call.

sections.h: At start-up, the reflective container loads Byte Buddy and writes classes
sections.html:
StartupLadder packs the demo box office into a JAR and starts it in fresh JVMs. It counts the lines that -Xlog:class+load prints, one per class the JVM loads, grouped by the source: each line names, as Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it did. On JDK 21:

setup                       loaded  archived  run-time  ready ms  wall ms
reflective + Byte Buddy       2207       953       156      1029     1307
    parsed from byte-buddy.jar 814, JDK proxies 30, defined from bytes 3, hidden 123
generated registry             991       834        51       266      418

The 1,216 extra classes are all machinery. 814 come from byte-buddy-1.18.17.jar: the library loads its own model of types, its matchers and its class writer before it can write one subclass. The costume department unpacks its whole sewing room to sew one costume. The 3 classes defined from bytes (source: __JVM_DefineClass__) are what it sewed: ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... and two $auxiliary$ helper classes, the @SuperCall callables for close and verify.

Then come 30 JDK proxy classes (__dynamic_proxy__), and only one of them is the booking stand-in. Every annotation you read through reflection is an object of a proxy class that the JDK writes for that annotation's type. So getAnnotation(Component.class) and isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class) make stand-ins too, and Byte Buddy uses a few proxies of its own inside. The 123 hidden classes are lambdas and method handles. A hidden class is one the JVM makes for its own use, which no class loader can find by name, and a method handle is a small JDK object that points at a method. Each lambda becomes a hidden class the first time its "ask the director" cue runs, as invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile showed. Since JDK 18, core reflection itself runs on method handles, so every reflective call path adds a few more.

Each of those classes is found, parsed and verified, the corner shop unpacking and checking every box again, then run in the interpreter, because nothing is hot yet. Every start is the cook's first day again. That's why ready, from the first line of main to the first ticket sold, was 1,029 ms against 266 ms. The machine was busy, and the times moved by a factor of two between runs. The reflective start was always several times slower, though, and the class counts barely moved: a later run gave 2,208 and 991.

None of this means Byte Buddy is slow. It does at every start what a compiler could have done once. So let's give that work to the compiler.

code.title: StartupLadder.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l03.demo; import workbench.container.l03.Container; import workbench.container.l03.Interception; import workbench.container.l03.RegistryGenerator; import workbench.container.l03.demo.app.DemoApp; import javax.tools.ToolProvider; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.stream.Collectors; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** * Starts the demo app in fresh JVMs: wired by the reflective container, then by a registry generated * "at build time" (here, at the start of this demo), each with and without a dynamic AppCDS archive. * Class counts come from -Xlog:class+load and barely change between runs; times change a lot. */ public class StartupLadder { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--reflective")) { // the child JVM's entry point long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String result = DemoApp.run(new Container(DemoApp.COMPONENTS)); System.out.println(String.format("ready: %s in %.0f ms", result, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6)); return; } Path demo = location(StartupLadder.class); // build/classes/java/demo Path out = Files.createDirectories(demo.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("cap4")); // container/build/cap4 Path jar = buildApp(demo, out); List<String> classPath = new ArrayList<>(List.of(jar.toString())); for (String entry : System.getProperty("java.class.path").split(java.io.File.pathSeparator)) { String name = Path.of(entry).getFileName().toString(); if (name.startsWith("byte-buddy-") || name.startsWith("kotlin-stdlib-")) classPath.add(entry); } String cp = String.join(java.io.File.pathSeparator, classPath); Files.writeString(out.resolve("classpath.txt"), cp); // for the AppCDS and AOT cache commands System.out.printf("JDK %s, app and class path in %s%n", Runtime.version(), out); System.out.printf("%-26s %7s %9s %9s %9s %8s%n", "setup", "loaded", "archived", "run-time", "ready ms", "wall ms"); String reflective = StartupLadder.class.getName(); String generated = "workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart"; row("reflective + Byte Buddy", List.of(), cp, reflective, "--reflective"); row("generated registry", List.of(), cp, generated); for (String[] setup : new String[][] {{"reflective", reflective, "--reflective"}, {"generated", generated, ""}}) { Path jsa = out.resolve(setup[0] + ".jsa"); // training run: the archive is written at exit Files.deleteIfExists(jsa); run(List.of("-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=" + jsa), cp, setup[1], setup[2]); row(setup[0] + ", AppCDS", List.of("-XX:SharedArchiveFile=" + jsa), cp, setup[1], setup[2]); } } /** One logged run for the class counts, then one quiet run for the times. */ static void row(String name, List<String> flags, String cp, String main, String... args) throws Exception { List<String> logged = new ArrayList<>(flags); logged.add("-Xlog:class+load"); List<String> lines = run(logged, cp, main, args); List<String> sources = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")) .map(l -> l.substring(l.indexOf(" source: ") + 9)).toList(); long archived = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.startsWith("shared objects file")).count(); // "(top)": AppCDS long proxies = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.equals("__dynamic_proxy__")).count(); long fromBytes = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.equals("__JVM_DefineClass__")).count(); long hidden = sources.stream().filter(s -> !s.startsWith("jrt:") && !s.startsWith("file:") && !s.startsWith("shared") && !s.startsWith("__dynamic") && !s.equals("__JVM_DefineClass__")).count(); long byteBuddyJar = sources.stream().filter(s -> s.contains("byte-buddy-")).count(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String ready = run(flags, cp, main, args).stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith("ready: ")).findFirst().orElseThrow(); long wall = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-26s %7d %9d %9d %9s %8d%n", name, sources.size(), archived, proxies + fromBytes + hidden, ready.replaceAll(".* in (\\S+) ms", "$1"), wall); System.out.printf(" parsed from byte-buddy.jar %d, JDK proxies %d, defined from bytes %d, hidden %d%n", byteBuddyJar, proxies, fromBytes, hidden); } static List<String> run(List<String> flags, String cp, String main, String... args) throws Exception { List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(flags); cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", cp, main)); Arrays.stream(args).filter(a -> !a.isEmpty()).forEach(cmd::add); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> output = p.inputReader().lines().toList(); if (p.waitFor() != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("child failed: " + cmd + "\n" + String.join("\n", output)); return output; } /** The "build": generate the registry, compile it with javac, and pack everything into one JAR (CDS wants JARs). */ static Path buildApp(Path demo, Path out) throws Exception { Path src = Files.createDirectories(out.resolve("gen-src/workbench/container/l03/demo/gen")); Files.writeString(src.resolve("AppRegistry.java"), RegistryGenerator.generate("workbench.container.l03.demo.gen", "AppRegistry", DemoApp.COMPONENTS)); Files.writeString(src.resolve("GeneratedStart.java"), """ package workbench.container.l03.demo.gen; public final class GeneratedStart { public static void main(String[] args) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); String result = workbench.container.l03.demo.app.DemoApp.run(new AppRegistry()); System.out.println(String.format("ready: %s in %.0f ms", result, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6)); } } """); Path genClasses = Files.createDirectories(out.resolve("gen-classes")); int status = ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler().run(null, null, null, "--release", "21", "-proc:none", "-nowarn", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "-d", genClasses.toString(), src.resolve("AppRegistry.java").toString(), src.resolve("GeneratedStart.java").toString()); if (status != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("javac failed on the generated registry"); Path jar = out.resolve("app.jar"); try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream zip = new JarOutputStream(file)) { add(zip, demo, "workbench/container/l03/demo"); // the demo app and this class add(zip, location(Container.class), "workbench/container/l03"); // the container, Java half add(zip, location(Interception.class), "workbench/container/l03"); // the container, Kotlin half add(zip, genClasses, "workbench/container/l03/demo/gen"); // what the generator wrote } return jar; } static void add(JarOutputStream zip, Path root, String pkg) throws IOException { try (Stream<Path> files = Files.walk(root.resolve(pkg))) { for (Path f : files.filter(f -> f.toString().endsWith(".class")).sorted().collect(Collectors.toList())) { String name = root.relativize(f).toString().replace('\\', '/'); if (pkg.equals("workbench/container/l03") && name.substring(pkg.length() + 1).contains("/")) continue; // no subpackages zip.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(name)); zip.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)); zip.closeEntry(); } } } static Path location(Class<?> c) throws Exception { return Path.of(c.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); } }

sections.h: Write the wiring out at build time: generate the registry
sections.html:
Everything the reflective container works out at start-up depends only on the classes, and the classes are fixed when the program is built. So do the work then. Picture the front-of-house manager from lesson 1 writing the evening's running order the afternoon before. On the night, nobody reads a single card; the crew follows the sheet.

RegistryGenerator is that afternoon. It runs the same BeanGraph from lesson 1 at build time: it picks the constructors, orders the graph and checks for loops, and a loop now fails the build instead of the start. Then it prints a Java class that does the wiring with plain new calls, and the lab's test compiles that class with javac, the way a build would. It prints source rather than class files on purpose. Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API showed the theatre's own printing press for class files, but source is easier to read, and javac checks it for us.

Each singleton gets a holder class, as lesson 1 promised:

Java
private static final class PriceList_Holder {
    static final PriceList INSTANCE = new PriceList(SeatingPlan_Holder.INSTANCE);
}
Kotlin
private object PriceListHolder {
    val INSTANCE = PriceList(SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE)    // a Kotlin object is a holder class too
}

The JVM initializes PriceList_Holder the first time get touches it: one dress rehearsal, under the class initialization lock from Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization. Its dependency is another holder, which the JVM initializes first. There is no volatile, no lock after the first call, and no map: get is a list of checks like if (type == PriceList.class). A prototype gets a factory method instead.

Interceptors become source too. For BookingClient, the generator writes RemoteBookingClient_Proxy implements BookingClient, and for ShowCloser it writes ShowCloser_Intercepted extends ShowCloser: the same stand-in and costume copy as lesson 2, printed in advance. The generator reads @Timed and @Retry while it runs and writes their values into the code, as in INTERCEPTION.chain(true, 3, BookingUnavailableException.class), so nothing reads an annotation when the program starts. Real frameworks do the same. Quarkus's container, ArC, generates subclasses like these while the application is built; Micronaut does the graph work while javac compiles; and Spring can generate its wiring as code ahead of time.

You give up two things. The set of components is fixed when you build: nothing can scan a plugin directory at start-up, or choose a part from a setting, unless the generator wrote code for it. And a holder fails for good. If BoxOffice's constructor throws on first use, the JVM marks BoxOffice_Holder as failed, and every later get throws NoClassDefFoundError until the program restarts. Lesson 1's cell would simply have tried again.

What depends only on your classes can be worked out once, when you build. Do it there, and leave the start only what's left.

Before we archive what's left, let's look inside a running container and count what it keeps.

sections.h: Look inside the running container: a histogram and a heap dump
sections.html:
Measure the running container from outside. Picture the warehouse from the Memory and GC track: the heap is its shared floor, and each object is a box with a label that names its class. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram runs a full GC and then counts the boxes on the floor by label. (jcmd is the JDK's tool for sending commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is that JVM's process id.) Here is the reflective container after one sale, one return and one closing, trimmed:

 num     #instances         #bytes  class name (module)
  99:            42            672  jdk.proxy2.$Proxy8 (jdk.proxy2)
 138:            13            312  workbench.container.l03.SingletonCell
 167:            14            224  jdk.proxy2.$Proxy2 (jdk.proxy2)
 247:             1            112  net.bytebuddy.dynamic.loading.ByteArrayClassLoader
 523:             1             32  workbench.container.l03.Container
 866:             1             16  jdk.proxy2.$Proxy6 (jdk.proxy2)
 910:             1             16  workbench.container.l03.ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$3cYlOLuY

Read it like a stock list. The 13 SingletonCells are the 14 components minus the one prototype, Basket. One $Proxy6 is the booking stand-in. One ByteArrayClassLoader holds the Byte Buddy subclass and its two helper classes, and one ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... is the closer itself. The other proxy objects are not parts of the box office at all. In this run, $Proxy2, with 14 instances, is the @Component annotation, one instance per component class. $Proxy8, with 42, is a proxy Byte Buddy uses to call JDK methods that don't exist on every Java version it supports. There were 119 proxy objects in all, and one of them was a part of the box office.

The histogram says what is alive, not who holds it. jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <file> writes every object and every reference between them to a file, 8 MB here, in the HPROF format that heap tools read. The JVM pauses while it writes, so on a busy program, take one only when you can afford a pause. Eclipse MAT, a free tool for reading heap dumps, can then show any object's path to GC roots. That's the cleaning crew's route from the Memory track: the notes it follows from the workers' desks and the noticeboard to the box. For the ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... object, the path should run through SingletonCell.instance and the container's singletons map to the Container, held by a local variable of the main thread.

The demo also proves it by letting go. It drops its only reference to the container and asks for a GC. Byte Buddy's class loader is collected, and with it the generated class. A class keeps its loader alive and an object keeps its class alive, so once the container was unreachable, the whole chain was. The plan for that box left the filing cabinet once no box made from it remained. The JDK proxy class stays loaded, because it was defined in the application class loader, which lives as long as the program, and Proxy caches it there. The annotation instances stay too, cached with the classes and methods they label.

The generated registry has a different root. Its singletons sit in static fields of holder classes, so they live as long as the class loader that loaded the registry. That's why the lab's tests load a fresh copy of the class for every test. And that registry leaves very little to make at start-up, which is exactly what an archive wants.

} System.out.println("after dropping the container:"); System.out.println(" Byte Buddy's class loader collected: " + (generatedLoader.get() == null)); System.out.println(" " + proxyClass + " still loaded: " + stillLoaded(proxyClass)); if (wait) { System.out.printf("Run the histogram again, then press Enter to exit.%n"); System.in.read(); } else { histogram(pid, proxyClass); } } /** The container's own lines of the histogram, then the proxy classes with live instances, grouped. */ static void histogram(long pid, String ourProxy) throws Exception { List<String> lines = jcmd(pid, "GC.class_histogram"); System.out.println(lines.get(1)); // the column headings lines.stream().filter(l -> l.matches(".*(\\.Container|SingletonCell|InterceptingHandler|SubclassBridge" + "|\\$ByteBuddy\\$\\w+|ByteArrayClassLoader|app\\.BoxOffice)( \\(.*)?$") || l.contains(" " + ourProxy + " ")).forEach(System.out::println); sections.h: Archive what's left: AppCDS on JDK 21, the AOT cache on JDK 25
sections.html:
Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache showed how to skip part of a start. Its shopkeeper keeps yesterday's filled shelves in the back room and wheels them out at opening time. An archive is a file of classes the JVM has already parsed and checked; at the next start, the JVM maps the file into memory instead of reading each class again. AppCDS, application class data sharing, puts your own classes in such an archive, and on JDK 21 one flag on a training run writes it. Apply it to both containers, and the last two rows of StartupLadder appear:

reflective, AppCDS            2145      2037       108       544      858
    parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 30, defined from bytes 3, hidden 75
generated, AppCDS              882       847        35       143      362
    parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 0, defined from bytes 0, hidden 35

AppCDS took Byte Buddy's 814 classes from the archive and nearly halved the reflective start. It couldn't take the classes made while the program runs. When the archive was written, JDK 21 printed Skipping jdk/proxy2/$Proxy3: Unsupported location for each of the 30 proxy classes. And the archived run still logs Byte Buddy's three classes as __JVM_DefineClass__: defined from bytes by its own class loader, at every start. So every start still writes and verifies them, and still runs the code that writes them. The generated registry has nothing of the kind. Its only classes made at start-up are 35 hidden ones for lambdas.

The AOT cache, Project Leyden's newer archive, goes further for the classes it can store. They arrive already loaded and linked, with the shopkeeper's notes from the training run about which code was busy. JEP 483 brought it in JDK 24, and JDK 25 made it a single step with -XX:AOTCacheOutput. Use JDK 25.0.4 or later, as that lesson explained. The limit on custom class loaders stays: the cache doesn't store the classes they define, so Byte Buddy's classes are made at every start either way.

The registry is also the shape GraalVM native image wants. GraalVM native image and Quarkus native pictured it as a pop-up stall built at a factory, which sells only what the factory packed. The registry has no reflection to declare and no classes defined at run time, which a closed world can't contain. (CRaC, the photo of the warm shop, sidesteps the question: a restored JVM already holds the classes Byte Buddy made before the photo.) That is the whole argument for build-time wiring in one sentence: the less a start has to discover, write and verify, the more of it a cache, an archive or a native build can do for you.

compare.title: A generated registry in Java, and the same idea written by hand in Kotlin

java.title: AppRegistry.java (generated, trimmed)
java.html: public final class AppRegistry implements Registry { private static final class SeatingPlan_Holder { static final SeatingPlan INSTANCE = new SeatingPlan(); } private static final class PriceList_Holder { static final PriceList INSTANCE = new PriceList(SeatingPlan_Holder.INSTANCE); } private static Basket new_Basket() { // a prototype return new Basket(PriceList_Holder.INSTANCE); } @Override public <T> T get(Class<T> type) { if (type == SeatingPlan.class) return type.cast(SeatingPlan_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == PriceList.class) return type.cast(PriceList_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == Basket.class) return type.cast(new_Basket()); throw new ContainerException("No component provides " + type.getSimpleName()); } }

kotlin.title: AppRegistry.kt (by hand)
kotlin.html: object AppRegistry { private object SeatingPlanHolder { val INSTANCE = SeatingPlan() } private object PriceListHolder { val INSTANCE = PriceList(SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE) } private fun newBasket() = Basket(PriceListHolder.INSTANCE) // a prototype @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun <T> get(type: Class<T>): T = when (type) { SeatingPlan::class.java -> SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE PriceList::class.java -> PriceListHolder.INSTANCE Basket::class.java -> newBasket() else -> throw ContainerException("No component provides ${type.simpleName}") } as T }

compare.note: Both compile to the same mechanism: one class per singleton whose static initializer builds it on first use, under the JVM's class initialization lock. A Kotlin object is that holder class, with its instance in a static INSTANCE field. The difference is who writes it. The Java one comes from a generator and is never edited; the Kotlin one is the kind of code Dagger, a build-time container, generates, written here by hand, which is fine for ten components and painful for eighty. You don't need by lazy here: it would work, but it adds a Lazy object per part and a volatile read per access to do what the class initialization lock already does.

worked.title: Design review: where does a setting go?

steps.say: A new requirement: on the theatre's test machine, the box office must use MockBookingClient instead of RemoteBookingClient, chosen by the property booking=mock (a setting passed on the command line as -Dbooking=mock). In the run-time container it's one filter before the graph is built, because the container learns its components at start-up anyway.
steps.code: List<Class<?>> components = new ArrayList<>(DemoApp.COMPONENTS); if ("mock".equals(System.getProperty("booking"))) { components.remove(RemoteBookingClient.class); // decided at start-up components.add(MockBookingClient.class); } Registry registry = new Container(components);

alt.html: val components = DemoApp.COMPONENTS.toMutableList() if (System.getProperty("booking") == "mock") { components -= RemoteBookingClient::class.java // decided at start-up components += MockBookingClient::class.java } val registry: Registry = Container(components)

steps.say: The generated registry has no start-up graph to change. One option is to generate one registry per setup and choose at the edge of the program, where it starts. Each registry stays plain code, and the setting picks a class, not a graph.
steps.code: String source = RegistryGenerator.generate("theatre.gen", "TestRegistry", testComponents); // ...and LiveRegistry from the live list, both at build time Registry registry = "mock".equals(System.getProperty("booking")) ? new TestRegistry() : new LiveRegistry();

steps.say: Check the costs. Two registries double the generated code and ship the mock inside the real program. If the choice really is fixed per machine, a build-time setting is cleaner: build the test copy from the test list. Quarkus draws exactly this line between build-time configuration, fixed in the built program, and run-time configuration, read at start-up.

Write the decision down in one sentence a reviewer can check: "The booking implementation is chosen per build, so each build wires one graph; a run-time property may change the booking service's address and timeouts, never which class is wired." That sentence is the design review's answer, and the test that proves it is the lab's: the generated registry wires the same graph as the reflective one, for each list.

lab.title: Generate the registry
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Everything else in l03 is the finished container from lessons 1 and 2, plus Registry (what both containers offer) and ProxySource, which writes the interceptor classes as source. Skim ProxySource.emit once.
Read GeneratedCode in the test folder: it is the "build". It compiles your source with javac and loads it in a fresh class loader for every test, so each test gets fresh singletons.

In RegistryGenerator.generate, build a BeanGraph, take its creation order, and start with header(...). For each component, write a holder class for a singleton or a factory method for a prototype, using the helpers holder, factory, beanType and newExpression.

Run the tests until all seven pass. If one says the generated source does not compile, read the numbered listing it prints. Then run GenerateDemo and read what your code writes for the demo box office.

Container.scopeOf(c) is package-private in Container, and RegistryGenerator is in the same package, so you can call it.

The concurrency test passes as soon as your holders are right, with no lock in your code. If you can say why (one thread runs a class's static initializer while the others wait), you have the main idea of this lesson.
A test that sees NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ...Holder means a constructor threw inside a holder. The first failure in the output names the real exception.

drill.title: A holder-based registry by hand
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Without a generator, write a registry for three components: SeatingPlan() (singleton), PriceList(SeatingPlan) (singleton) and Basket(PriceList) (prototype), with a get(Class<T>) that throws for anything else. Then compare. Which line makes PriceList safe when eight threads ask first?

answer.html: public final class BoxOfficeRegistry { private static final class SeatingPlanHolder { static final SeatingPlan INSTANCE = new SeatingPlan(); } private static final class PriceListHolder { // initialized once, under the JVM's lock static final PriceList INSTANCE = new PriceList(SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE); } private static Basket newBasket() { // a prototype: new every time return new Basket(PriceListHolder.INSTANCE); } public <T> T get(Class<T> type) { if (type == SeatingPlan.class) return type.cast(SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE); if (type == PriceList.class) return type.cast(PriceListHolder.INSTANCE); if (type == Basket.class) return type.cast(newBasket()); throw new IllegalArgumentException("No component provides " + type.getSimpleName()); } }

alt.html: object BoxOfficeRegistry { private object SeatingPlanHolder { val INSTANCE = SeatingPlan() } private object PriceListHolder { val INSTANCE = PriceList(SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE) } // once, under the JVM's lock private fun newBasket() = Basket(PriceListHolder.INSTANCE) // a prototype: new every time @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun <T> get(type: Class<T>): T = when (type) { SeatingPlan::class.java -> SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE PriceList::class.java -> PriceListHolder.INSTANCE Basket::class.java -> newBasket() else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("No component provides ${type.simpleName}") } as T }

recap: Measure both clocks. JMH's -prof gc gave 0 B/op for a direct call and for generated interceptor code (escape analysis removed its objects), about 160 for a Byte Buddy subclass and 208 for a JDK proxy. Bytes per call were far steadier than time, and per call they only matter in hot loops.

At start-up the reflective container loaded 2,207 classes against 991 for generated wiring: 814 from Byte Buddy's JAR, 30 JDK proxy classes (mostly annotation instances), 3 generated subclasses and helpers, and over a hundred hidden classes.

A generated registry does the graph work at build time and wires with new: a holder class per singleton (lazy and thread-safe through the class initialization lock), a factory per prototype, identity checks in get, and interceptors as source. A loop fails the build.

jcmd GC.class_histogram shows what the container keeps alive; a heap dump and its path to GC roots show who holds it. Dropping the container freed Byte Buddy's loader and classes; the JDK proxy class and the annotation instances stayed.

AppCDS and the AOT cache archive classes from JARs, not classes made at run time: the 30 proxies are skipped, and Byte Buddy's classes come from a custom loader. Generated wiring leaves almost nothing to make at start-up, which also suits native image.

Where build-time wiring stops: the set of parts is fixed when you build, and a holder whose constructor throws stays broken until restart. Run-time wiring keeps that flexibility and pays for it at every start.

explain.prompt: Design review. A sceptical reviewer says: "Our services wire everything by reflection and proxies at start-up, and it works. Generating code is extra build machinery. Why should we ever wire at build time?" Defend the design you built across these three lessons, with the numbers you measured, and say when you would not do it.
explain.answer: Both containers compute the same thing: the same constructors, the same order, the same interceptor chains. The only question is when. At run time it costs every start: here 2,207 classes against 991, because the container loads Byte Buddy, reads annotations through proxies, writes and verifies subclasses, and runs all of it cold in the interpreter. AppCDS nearly halved that, but it can't archive the proxies or Byte Buddy's classes, so every start still makes them. Generated wiring moves the work to the build: a loop fails the build, the start runs only holder initializers, the per-call path allocates nothing after inlining, and the result has no reflection for native image to declare. What it costs: a generator in the build, a set of components fixed per build, and holders that fail for good if a constructor throws, so constructors must be trivial. I wouldn't do it for a program that starts once a week, runs for days, and needs plugins or parts chosen at start-up; there, reflection's flexibility is worth a slower start. I would for programs that start often, run as many small copies at once, or must be answering within a second or two of starting.

deeper.html:
What a production container adds to the one you built, roughly in the order you would need it:

  • Lifecycle callbacks: @PostConstruct after injection, and @PreDestroy at shutdown, run in reverse creation order so a SalesBook closes after the BoxOffice that writes to it.
  • Qualifiers (@Named, @Qualifier) for two implementations of one interface, and matching by generic type, so Repository<Show> and Repository<Seat> are different dependencies.
  • More scopes: one instance per request or per user session, with a client proxy that forwards each call to the right instance for the current scope.
  • Configuration injection, with type conversion and checks, split into build-time and run-time settings.
  • Interceptor ordering by priority, decorators, and events between components.
  • Lookups (Provider<T>, Instance<T>) for edges that must be followed at call time.
  • Test support: swapping one component for a fake without rewriting the graph.
  • Error messages that print the whole dependency path, not only the loop.

The way the generator runs matters too. This lab runs it as a separate step on compiled classes, which is close to what Quarkus does during its build. Dagger and Micronaut run theirs as annotation processors inside javac, so the generated classes are compiled with your code and IDEs can show them, but the processor sees source-level elements instead of loaded classes. Spring's AOT processing starts the application's wiring during the build and writes what it found as code.

For the start itself, the next levers after this lesson are the ones the Startup track covered: an AOT cache trained on representative work, then native image if memory per copy or start time is still the limit. Generated wiring makes both easier, because there is less left for the JVM to discover.
